title: .NET architecture capstone -- Clean Architecture, microservices trade-offs, review
exp: The final .NET day ties every prior day into an architecture-level conversation -- the kind of question a Lead I candidate gets asked after the trivia is done: 'how would you structure a new service, and why.'
pts: Clean Architecture / Onion Architecture: dependencies point INWARD -- the Domain layer (entities, business rules) has zero dependencies on anything else; Application layer (use cases, interfaces) depends only on Domain; Infrastructure (EF Core, external APIs) and Presentation (API controllers) depend on Application/Domain, never the reverse.

The practical test for whether this is actually followed: can you swap EF Core for Dapper, or swap SQL Server for PostgreSQL, by changing ONLY the Infrastructure layer, with zero changes to Domain or Application code? If not, a dependency is pointing the wrong way somewhere.

Repository pattern revisited (from Day 6/7's EF Core discussion) in the Clean Architecture context: the Application layer defines an IOrderRepository INTERFACE (what operations are needed), and Infrastructure provides the EF Core-based IMPLEMENTATION -- this is what actually enables swapping the data access technology without touching business logic.

MediatR and the CQRS-lite pattern (Commands for writes, Queries for reads, each handled by a dedicated Handler class) is a common way to implement the Application layer's use cases -- keeps each use case's logic isolated in its own small class rather than accumulating dozens of methods in a single bloated service class.

Monolith vs microservices is a team-size and deployment-independence question, not a default technical preference -- a well-structured Clean Architecture monolith with clear internal module boundaries can be split into microservices later IF the boundaries were designed thoughtfully; a poorly-structured monolith with tangled dependencies cannot be cleanly split regardless of how badly a team wants microservices.

Domain Events (an entity raising an event like OrderApproved that other parts of the system react to, often dispatched via MediatR's notification pattern) decouple side effects (send an email, update a read model, trigger a downstream integration) from the core transaction that caused them -- avoiding a single service method that directly orchestrates five unrelated side effects inline.

Vertical Slice Architecture (organizing code by FEATURE -- everything for 'ApproveOrder' lives together -- rather than by TECHNICAL LAYER -- all controllers together, all services together, all repositories together) is a genuine alternative to strict Clean Architecture layering, trading some architectural purity for the practical benefit that a single feature's code is easy to find and reason about as one unit.

The interview-ready synthesis: architecture patterns aren't dogma to apply uniformly -- they're tools to manage complexity and enable specific kinds of change (swapping infrastructure, testing in isolation, splitting a monolith later). Choosing Clean Architecture, Vertical Slices, or a simpler pragmatic structure should be justified by the SPECIFIC change-tolerance the project actually needs, not applied because it's the 'correct' pattern in the abstract.
pr: Take a service method that directly calls repository.Save(), emailService.Send(), and auditLog.Write() inline, and refactor it to use a domain event so the side effects are decoupled from the core operation

viz.cap: Clean Architecture dependency direction -- everything points inward toward Domain, never outward

qa.q: What is the practical test for whether a codebase is actually following Clean Architecture's dependency rule, versus just having folders named Domain/Application/Infrastructure?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Can you swap the data access technology (EF Core to Dapper) or the database engine (SQL Server to PostgreSQL) by changing ONLY code inside the Infrastructure layer, with zero changes required in Domain or Application code? If the Domain layer references EF Core attributes, or the Application layer directly instantiates a DbContext instead of depending on a repository interface, the dependency is pointing the wrong way regardless of what the folders are named -- the folder structure alone doesn't enforce the actual architectural boundary.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transient creates a new instance on every request; Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request container; Singleton lives for the app domain lifespan. Capturing a Scoped service inside a Singleton captures the DbContext across requests, causing concurrency bugs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Instantiating new HttpClient() instances manually causes socket exhaustion in OS TIME_WAIT state under high concurrency. Fix: register typed clients with IHttpClientFactory to manage handler lifetimes and DNS refresh.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** IHttpClientFactory prevents socket leaks and manages DNS rotation, but requires explicit Polly retry and circuit breaker policies to prevent cascade failures during downstream outages.

qa.q: How does the Repository pattern from the EF Core day connect specifically to Clean Architecture's goals?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** The Application layer defines an interface like IOrderRepository describing WHAT data operations a use case needs, without knowing or caring HOW they're implemented. The Infrastructure layer provides the concrete EF Core-based implementation. This is precisely what allows swapping EF Core for a different technology later -- the Application layer's code never changes, since it only ever depended on the interface, not the concrete implementation. Without this interface boundary, Application code calling EF Core's DbContext directly would need to change if the underlying data access technology ever changed.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transient creates a new instance on every request; Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request container; Singleton lives for the app domain lifespan. Capturing a Scoped service inside a Singleton captures the DbContext across requests, causing concurrency bugs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Instantiating new HttpClient() instances manually causes socket exhaustion in OS TIME_WAIT state under high concurrency. Fix: register typed clients with IHttpClientFactory to manage handler lifetimes and DNS refresh.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** IHttpClientFactory prevents socket leaks and manages DNS rotation, but requires explicit Polly retry and circuit breaker policies to prevent cascade failures during downstream outages.

qa.q: What does Domain Events / MediatR's notification pattern buy you that a single method directly calling five side-effect methods inline doesn't?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Decoupling: the core business operation (ApproveOrderHandler approving an order) doesn't need to know or care that approving an order should also send an email, update a read model, and notify a downstream system -- it just raises an OrderApprovedEvent and moves on. Each side effect lives in its own independent handler that subscribes to that event. Adding a NEW side effect later (say, logging the approval to an audit system) means adding a new handler class, with zero changes to the original approval logic -- versus having to open and modify the original method to bolt on one more inline call every time a new side effect is needed.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular Signals maintain an internal reactive dependency graph (ReactiveNode). When a signal value updates, it marks dependent computed nodes as stale without running change detection immediately. Evaluation happens lazily when read, updating only impacted DOM bindings.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Writing to signals inside an effect() can trigger infinite reactive loops or untracked state dependencies. Fix: use computed() or linkedSignal() for derived state sync, keeping effect() strictly for un-tracked side effects like logging or localStorage.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Signals provide fine-grained, synchronous reactivity without Zone.js overhead, but require learning new primitives (input(), output(), model()) compared to classic RxJS BehaviorSubjects.

qa.q: How would you decide between strict Clean Architecture layering and Vertical Slice Architecture for a new service?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Clean Architecture's layer-based organization pays off most when the SAME domain logic is genuinely likely to be exposed through multiple different infrastructure choices, or when strict testability-in-isolation of business rules from any framework concern is a priority. Vertical Slice Architecture pays off when features are largely independent of each other and the team values being able to open one folder and see everything related to 'ApproveOrder' in one place, rather than hunting across Controllers/, Services/, Repositories/ folders for the pieces of one feature. Neither is universally correct -- the decision should be driven by which kind of future change (swapping infrastructure vs. quickly locating and modifying one feature) the project is more likely to need, not by which pattern is currently more fashionable.
